strengths: The paper addresses an important and understudied problem: evaluating NLP-assisted qualitative coding in realistic collaborative configurations rather than evaluating each tool only in isolation.
The study is ambitious in scope, comparing three system families—topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM-based labeling—across two structurally and semantically different datasets.

The evaluation framework is multidimensional, combining lexical and semantic consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, human-rated correctness, and post-task interviews. This is more informative than accuracy alone for interactive theme discovery.

The authors attempt to control some technical variation by using shared initial partitions, fixed topic-model hyperparameters, and common datasets across conditions, and they provide substantial corpus analysis in Appendix A.
The mixed-methods component is valuable: participant experiences help explain quantitative patterns, such as distrust caused by limited control and the relative usefulness of synchronous discussion.
Appendices improve reproducibility by documenting system operations, LLM prompts, model configuration, compute requirements, dataset statistics, and the interview script.
The paper is generally clearly written, with explicit research questions and useful conceptual figures describing the consistency and cohesiveness measures.

The findings are appropriately nuanced in places, acknowledging that effects interact with dataset characteristics and system affordances rather than claiming a universal advantage for synchronous coding.
weaknesses: The central comparison has a major construct-validity confound: synchronous conditions use three-person groups, while asynchronous conditions are individual coders. Any observed advantage may reflect having three coders, more total labor, or group aggregation rather than synchronous interaction itself. A proper comparison would include equal-size asynchronous groups or nominal-group controls whose independent codebooks are consolidated after coding.

The asynchronous condition does not fully realize the construct described in the introduction. The paper says asynchronous coders independently code before consolidating results, but the analyses evaluate individual codebooks and do not report an asynchronous consolidation stage.

Participant order is confounded with condition: participants who did both always performed asynchronous coding first and at most one synchronous task. Practice, familiarity with the system/dataset, fatigue, or carryover could therefore improve synchronous performance. The paper does not describe randomization or counterbalancing.

The number of independent experimental units is small and inconsistently reported. The text says three asynchronous and three synchronous experiments per system but states that there are 15 experiments total; the table sample sizes, number of groups per cell, participant allocation, and group composition are also unclear.

The statistical analysis risks pseudoreplication. Two-sample t-tests appear to treat themes or document pairs as independent observations even though they are nested within a small number of coders/groups. Experiment-level inference, mixed-effects models, or permutation tests are needed, along with exact n, confidence intervals, and effect sizes.

There are many significance tests across datasets, metrics, systems, and subsets without an explicit multiple-comparison correction. The label 'near statistically significant with p ≈ 0.05' is not a well-defined inferential category.

The consistency metric uses each theme's maximum similarity to themes in another codebook. Unless matching is constrained to be one-to-one, multiple themes can align to the same partner and inflate agreement. Jaccard and centroid measures are also sensitive to theme cardinality and overly broad themes.

Embedding-based cohesiveness is not a direct measure of conceptual quality. High intra-theme similarity and low inter-theme similarity can indicate redundancy or fragmentation, and the post hoc top-25% analysis may favor systems with particular weight distributions. Human validation of these structural metrics is limited.

The correctness evaluation is under-specified. It is unclear how the reported F1 score is derived from binary judgments of sampled pairs, what annotation guidelines and blinding procedures were used, or how the 1,200 pairs correspond to '200 per experimental setting' across the 12 dataset–system–modality cells. Krippendorff's alpha of 0.632 indicates only moderate agreement.

Generalization is limited because only one implementation represents each method family, the LLM is a relatively small Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct model, and both datasets are English political/advertising text. The LLM system also offers fewer interactive operations than the other tools, confounding model family with interface affordances.

The qualitative analysis does not report how many participants were interviewed, how they were selected, how interview themes were coded, or whether any reliability checks were performed. Interview quotes can establish user perceptions but cannot independently validate causal effects on coding quality.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, particularly the conclusion that collaboration modality is a demonstrated significant determinant of output quality. The promise to release code and annotations is welcome, but no repository or persistent artifact is provided in the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and understudied problem: how collaborative workflows affect NLP-assisted qualitative coding, rather than evaluating interactive systems only in isolation.
The study is reasonably ambitious in scope, comparing three system categories—topic modeling, relational inference, and an LLM-based workflow—across two contrasting text corpora.
The proposed evaluation framework is valuable in spirit because it examines multiple dimensions of code-book quality: consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, correctness, and user experience.
The mixed-methods design combines quantitative metrics with semi-structured interviews, producing potentially useful design recommendations for human-in-the-loop qualitative-analysis tools.
The appendices provide substantial implementation detail, including corpus statistics, system settings, participant questions, LLM prompts, and hyperparameters.
The dataset analysis is informative and helps explain why collaboration effects may differ between short, semantically homogeneous tweets and longer, more formulaic advertisements.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded. The asynchronous condition uses one coder per experiment and appears to include no asynchronous reconciliation, while the synchronous condition uses three coders discussing themes in real time. This manipulates group size, total labor, and presence of discussion simultaneously, so it cannot isolate synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration. The paper would need true asynchronous teams with independent coding followed by consolidation, or it must explicitly reframe the study as solo coding versus synchronous group coding.

The number of independent experimental units is very small and is reported inconsistently. The text refers to three synchronous experiments and 15 total experiments, but later discusses 'the two synchronous groups.' With only two or three groups per system-condition cell, group-level statistical conclusions are inherently fragile.

The statistical analysis appears to use documents or themes as independent observations in unpaired t-tests, despite their being nested within coders, groups, systems, and datasets. There is no cluster-aware model, mixed-effects analysis, permutation test, or bootstrap at the group level, and no correction for the many comparisons. The use of 'near statistically significant' marking for p approximately 0.05 is also inappropriate.

There is an order and participation confound: participants who completed both conditions always performed asynchronous coding first and could participate in at most one synchronous experiment. Counterbalancing and assignment procedures are not described, so learning, fatigue, and prior exposure cannot be ruled out.

The consistency metrics can overstate agreement. Maximum one-to-many matching lets several themes align to the same target theme and does not penalize unmatched or duplicate themes. Jaccard overlap over fully propagated assignments may also reflect each system's propagation mechanism rather than genuine coder agreement.

Cohesiveness and distinctiveness are proxies rather than validated measures of coding quality. Highly coherent themes may be overly narrow or generic, while the top-25% subset is defined using system-specific weights or distances, making cross-system comparisons less straightforward.

The correctness evaluation is under-specified. The paper does not clearly describe the annotation rubric, how F1 was computed, or how the manual labels constitute a reference standard. Inter-annotator agreement is only moderate (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.632), and the reported correctness analysis appears to cover only the Covid dataset, with no comparable Climate analysis.

The systems differ substantially in user control—for example, the LLM system mainly permits definition editing, whereas the other systems support merging, splitting, or relational refinement. Thus system-by-collaboration interactions may be caused by interface affordances rather than the NLP approach itself. The per-codebook selection of LLM prompt templates also introduces an additional tuning difference.

The qualitative interview analysis is not reported with a systematic coding procedure, reliability measure, or theme frequency analysis, so the interview findings remain suggestive rather than independently verifiable evidence.

Although the appendices are helpful, reproducibility would still require the code-book matching implementation, random seeds, software versions, annotation interface and rubric, participant allocation, and a working artifact URL. The promised release of code and annotations cannot be verified from the manuscript.

The conclusions are stronger than the evidence. Many reported differences are nonsignificant or reverse direction across datasets and systems, and the paper provides no omnibus test of collaboration modality. The current results are best interpreted as exploratory patterns, not evidence that collaboration modality is a significant causal factor.

Generalizability remains limited to two English datasets, three selected tools, one small open-weight LLM, and participants who are primarily NLP or computational social science researchers rather than necessarily domain-expert qualitative analysts.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important gap: NLP-assisted qualitative coding tools are usually evaluated in isolation, whereas real analysis is often collaborative.

It proposes a multidimensional evaluation framework covering consistency, semantic cohesiveness/distinctiveness, correctness, and participant experience, using established measures such as Jaccard similarity, S-BERT embeddings, GWET's AC1, and manual reliability checks.

The study has useful breadth: three distinct NLP paradigms, synchronous and asynchronous configurations, and two structurally different corpora, with substantial corpus-level characterization in the appendix.

The mixed-methods design combines quantitative experiments with semi-structured interviews, giving both outcome measures and insight into why particular systems or collaboration modes help or hinder coders.

The findings are appropriately nuanced in much of the analysis: synchronous work does not universally improve every dimension, and effects vary by system, dataset, and evaluation metric. The observations about limited LLM control and computational cost are especially practical.

Reproducibility is stronger than in many user studies: the appendices provide topic-model settings, system operations, dataset statistics, LLM prompts, and hyperparameters, and the authors state that code and annotation results will be released.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded: synchronous conditions use three-person groups while asynchronous conditions use one coder each. Differences may therefore reflect the number of coders, combined expertise, or person-hours rather than collaboration modality alone. The asynchronous setting is also described as individual coding followed by consolidation, but the evaluated protocol appears to contain only independent individual coding.

There are very few independent treatment units—two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system. If significance tests are conducted over themes or document pairs, those observations are nested within coding groups and cannot be treated as independent experimental replicates. Group-level analyses, permutation tests, or mixed-effects models, along with effect sizes and confidence intervals, are needed.

The many t-tests across systems, datasets, metrics, and sub-analyses are reported without a clear analysis unit or multiple-comparison correction. With only two synchronous groups, the statistical significance and generalizability of the starred differences are uncertain.

Only one implementation is selected for each NLP paradigm, and the systems differ substantially in interaction affordances. In particular, the LLM system offers much weaker intervention support than the topic-model and relational systems, so differences attributed to NLP approach may partly reflect interface or workflow design.

Several evaluation choices require sensitivity analysis. Maximum theme matching can inflate consistency and allow one-to-many alignment, while cohesiveness scores may depend on theme count, theme size, and granularity. Codebook sizes and model-dependent top-25% subsets should be reported and controlled for.

Correctness appears to be evaluated only on the COVID dataset, and the exact ground-truth mapping, F1 computation, sampling procedure, and annotation rubric are not fully specified. Krippendorff's alpha of 0.632 indicates only moderate agreement, and the 1,200 judgments remain nested within systems, groups, and themes.

Important procedural details are missing or unclear, including randomization and assignment of participants, balancing of prior expertise, time/effort controls, group-communication mechanics, LLM decoding parameters such as temperature and maximum output length, and whether synchronous participants benefited from prior asynchronous experience.
The interview analysis would benefit from a clearer description of how themes were derived, how many interviews were conducted, and whether the qualitative coding was validated by multiple analysts.

The title and abstract make a somewhat stronger causal and cross-setting claim than the evidence supports. The most defensible interpretation is a descriptive ecological comparison of particular tool configurations, with promising but contingent findings; the limitations section should explicitly discuss the headcount/modality confound and statistical-power limitations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and understudied problem in NLP-supported qualitative research: how synchronous versus asynchronous coding configurations affect resulting code-books rather than evaluating tools only in isolation.

It proposes a broad, mixed-methods evaluation framework covering consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and correctness, and triangulates quantitative metrics with semi-structured interviews and design recommendations.

The comparison spans three methodologically distinct systems—topic modeling, relational concept inference, and LLM-based labeling—and two structurally different corpora, giving useful evidence about where findings do and do not transfer.

The protocol is comparatively detailed and reproducibility-oriented: it standardizes initial topic models or clusters, reports hyperparameters and prompt templates, describes coding procedures, and states that code and experimental data are publicly available.
Correctness is evaluated on stratified human judgments rather than only central or easy documents, using two annotators with a third tie-breaker and reported inter-annotator agreement.

The paper is clearly written and generally presents nuanced results, including cases where asynchronous coding performs similarly or better and cases where system intervention capabilities mediate the effect of collaboration.
weaknesses: The decisive limitation is statistical unit-of-analysis. There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders per system–dataset combination, while the reported t-tests appear to treat themes or document pairs as independent observations. This is pseudoreplication: themes are nested within code-books, coders participate repeatedly, and group-level effects are tested from very few independent groups. Mixed-effects models or group-level randomization tests with confidence intervals are needed.

The collaboration conditions are confounded with labor and process. Synchronous groups contain three coders, whereas asynchronous outcomes are produced by one coder each; without matching person-hours, effort, or redundancy, the study cannot cleanly attribute differences to discussion modality rather than simply having more people contribute.

Order is also confounded because asynchronous work was always performed first and synchronous participation was restricted to at most one experiment. Learning, fatigue, and prior exposure to the tools are not counterbalanced or modeled.

The asynchronous construct has limited ecological validity as implemented. Although the paper describes asynchronous coding as independent coding followed by consolidation, the evaluated asynchronous code-books appear to come from single coders and do not test the consolidation strategies commonly used in real asynchronous workflows.

The consistency metric uses an unconstrained maximum best match between themes, which can inflate agreement when multiple themes match the same target and when code-books contain different numbers of themes. A constrained one-to-one alignment and sensitivity analyses by theme count would strengthen the metric.

Cohesiveness and distinctiveness are embedding-dependent proxies rather than directly validated measures of interpretive quality, and they can be affected by corpus composition, document coverage, and cluster breadth. The correctness analysis also relies on subjective post hoc judgments with only moderate agreement (Krippendorff's alpha of 0.632 and 0.696), and Figure 4 lacks confidence intervals or a corresponding detailed results table.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially statements that collaboration modality 'significantly affects' quality and that dataset characteristics independently drive performance. With two datasets, many uncorrected significance tests, and post hoc corpus comparisons, the findings should be framed primarily as descriptive and exploratory rather than causal or broadly generalizable.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and understudied problem: how collaboration modality affects human-in-the-loop qualitative coding systems, with clear relevance to NLP, computational social science, and HCI.
It is ambitious in scope, comparing systems from three methodological families—topic modeling, relational concept learning, and LLMs—across two structurally different datasets.
The evaluation combines several complementary perspectives: code-book consistency, intra-/inter-theme semantic structure, manual correctness assessment, and semi-structured user feedback.
The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, and Figures 1–3 helpfully explain the comparison conditions and metrics.

Reproducibility is strengthened by detailed appendices covering system operations, prompt templates, model configuration, corpus statistics, and the resulting code-books, along with a stated commitment to release code and experimental data.

The interaction findings are potentially useful: systems offering richer intervention opportunities appear to benefit more from synchronous discussion, while corpus characteristics may change which modality is preferable.
weaknesses: The central comparison has a major construct-validity problem. The asynchronous condition consists of three coders working independently, without the consolidation stage described in the introduction, while the synchronous condition produces one group code-book through discussion. The study therefore compares individual coding with group coding, not asynchronous collaboration with synchronous collaboration.

The number of independent observational units is very small: only three individual code-books and two group code-books per system–dataset condition. Treating individual theme matches or document assignments as independent observations in t-tests constitutes pseudoreplication; valid inference would need to account for nesting in code-books/groups or use group-level analyses with substantially more groups.

The statistical evidence is overstated. There are many uncorrected comparisons across systems, datasets, and metrics, and reports such as 'near statistically significant with p approximately 0.05' are not a substitute for confidence intervals, effect sizes, a prespecified analysis plan, and appropriate multiple-comparison treatment.

Collaboration modality is confounded with group process and labor: a synchronous group contains three people discussing the task, whereas an asynchronous output represents one person. The study does not control or report time on task, total annotation effort, discussion duration, or individual contributions.

Participant ordering introduces another confound: repeat participants always performed asynchronous experiments first and at most one synchronous experiment, so practice or familiarity with the system could explain synchronous gains. Randomization and counterbalancing are not described.

The consistency, cohesiveness, and distinctiveness metrics are sensitive to theme count, theme granularity, cluster size, and embedding geometry. They do not directly establish that themes are interpretable, valid, or useful; a human evaluation of the code-book schemata themselves is largely missing.

Correctness is assessed only for document-theme assignments on post-hoc samples, not for the quality of the discovered theme labels or conceptual structure. Inter-annotator agreement is moderate (Krippendorff's alpha 0.632 and 0.696), and the sampling and F1 computation need more detailed justification and uncertainty estimates.

Generalization claims are too broad for one implementation per system category, one relatively small 3B-parameter LLM, and two datasets that differ simultaneously in domain, length, size, formulaicity, readability, and semantic homogeneity. The corpus-specific recommendations in Section 5.4 are plausible but observational and post hoc.

The three systems are not configured or constrained equivalently—for example, different initial cluster/topic counts and dataset-specific auxiliary concepts—so observed system differences may reflect setup or external label availability rather than the underlying methodology.

The qualitative user study is under-reported: it is unclear how many participants were interviewed, how transcripts were analyzed, whether themes were independently coded, or how representative the quoted experiences are. The interviews are therefore better treated as anecdotal triangulation than as confirmatory evidence.

There is no manual-only, fully automated, or time-matched control condition, making it difficult to judge whether either setting improves absolute coding quality or merely changes agreement among users.

These issues are fixable—especially by reframing the comparison as individual versus synchronous group coding, adding more independent groups, using hierarchical or permutation-based inference, and controlling effort/order—but they are central enough that the current claims are not adequately supported for Findings.

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: how collaboration modality affects NLP-assisted qualitative coding in realistic research workflows, rather than evaluating interactive systems only in isolation.
Uses a triangulated evaluation combining consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, manual correctness assessment, corpus analysis, and semi-structured interviews.

Compares three methodologically distinct system families—a query-driven topic model, a relational concept-learning system, and an LLM-based coding system—which strengthens coverage of current interactive theme-discovery approaches.

Includes two deliberately contrasting English corpora, short semantically homogeneous COVID-19 tweets and longer more heterogeneous climate advertisements, and quantitatively characterizes their linguistic and semantic differences.
Produces nuanced, practically useful findings: the effect of collaboration depends on both system affordances and dataset characteristics, avoiding a one-size-fits-all recommendation.
Supports reproducibility through publicly promised code and experimental data, detailed appendices, prompt templates, hyperparameters, final codebooks, and corpus statistics.
The paper is clearly written, and the figures effectively explain theme alignment and the cohesiveness/distinctiveness measures.
weaknesses: The asynchronous condition has construct-validity limitations: it appears to be independent individual coding with no reported consolidation or asynchronous communication, despite the introduction defining asynchronous coding as independent coding followed by consolidation. The comparison therefore conflates collaboration modality with group-versus-individual work and collaboration dose.

Statistical inference does not clearly respect the unit of assignment. There are only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous individuals per system–dataset cell, while t-tests are reported over themes or assignments. These nested outputs are not independent, creating pseudoreplication; cluster-level bootstrap/permutation tests, hierarchical models, or confidence intervals are needed.

Possible order, selection, and effort confounds remain. Repeat participants always completed asynchronous work first, and the paper does not show that expertise, group composition, time on task, or fatigue were balanced across conditions.

Correctness evidence is tentative because it relies on post-hoc human judgment without a gold standard. Krippendorff's alpha is 0.632 for COVID tweets, below the commonly used 0.667 reliability threshold, and 0.696 for climate ads; the annotation rubric, blinding, tie-breaking procedure, and derivation of the F1 scores should be specified more fully.

The automated metrics have validity limits. Maximum Jaccard matching can overstate agreement when codebooks contain many themes and may not enforce one-to-one alignment, while embedding-based cohesion measures semantic dispersion rather than conceptual or label validity.

Generalizability is bounded by the two English corpora, one implementation per system category, and single small Llama 3.2 3B model. Conclusions about LLM cost and unreliability, in particular, may not transfer to stronger models or other domains.
